q: Which three plain-text formats does chapter 18 teach?
why: The chapter covers CSV, JSON and XML files.

q: What is the first step in reading a CSV file with the csv module?
options: Loading the whole file into one string and splitting it on commas
Calling json.loads on the text of the file
Making a reader from an open file and taking its rows
why: Reading a CSV file means making a reader from an open file and taking its rows.

q: What does csv.reader give back when it is given a file object opened in text mode?
options: An object that yields each row as a list of strings
A dictionary for every row, keyed by the first row
One string holding the whole file
A list of integers for the numeric columns
why: csv.reader takes a file object, or any iterable of lines, and yields each row as a list of strings.

q: After list(reader) has been stored in example_data, how is the cell in row 1, column 2 found?
why: The list is a list of rows, so the row index comes first and then the column index.

q: Why is line_num not always the number of records read?
options: A record that contains a newline inside quotes spans more than one line
It counts only the rows that hold numbers
It is reset to 0 each time a row is read
why: line_num counts the lines read so far, so a quoted newline makes it run ahead of the record count.

q: What does a program give to a csv writer to make a row?
options: A string of the whole line with commas already inserted
A dictionary of column names only
A list of the cell values
why: Writing a CSV file means making a writer around a file opened for writing and giving it lists.

q: Why is a file given to the csv module opened with newline=''?
options: So that the text layer does not translate the line terminator the module already wrote
So that the file is opened for reading and writing at once
So that the file contains no line terminators at all
So that the delimiter becomes a tab
why: With newline='' the module's own line terminator is not translated a second time.

q: Which keyword arguments of csv.writer make a tab-separated file with two newlines at the end of each row?
why: delimiter sets the character between cells and lineterminator the characters ending a row.

q: How does a program read a CSV file with a header row so that cells are found by column name?
options: With csv.reader and a try block
With csv.DictReader, which gives one dictionary per row
why: A file with a header row is read and written as dictionaries whose keys are the column names.

q: What does DictReader do when it is given a second argument with field names?
options: It raises a ValueError if the file has a header
It renames the columns of the file on disk
It ignores the first column of the file
It uses those names as keys and treats the first row of the file as data
why: Given field names, DictReader treats the first row of the file as data.

q: Which DictWriter method writes the field names as the first row?
why: writeheader writes the field names as the first row; writerow then takes dictionaries.

q: What do the csv options that the chapter leaves out cover?
options: Only the order of the columns
Only the encoding of the file
Quoting, detecting a format with the Sniffer, and error handling
Only the name of the file
why: The chapter does not use the options for quoting, format detection and error handling.

q: What does Project 13 of the chapter do?
options: It sorts every CSV file by its first column
It removes the first line from every CSV file in a folder
It converts every CSV file into JSON
It merges all CSV files into one
why: Project 13 removes the first line from every CSV file in a folder and is written in three steps.

q: How does Project 13 decide which row to skip?
options: It skips the row that holds text instead of numbers
It skips every row with an empty cell
It skips the row whose line_num is 1
why: The program skips the row whose line_num is 1 and writes the others to a file of the same name in a new folder.

q: What is JSON used for in the chapter?
options: Nested dictionaries and lists, read and written with the json module
Tables of rows with identical columns
Documents with one root element and attributes
why: JSON is the chapter's second format, for nested dictionaries and lists.

q: What do JSON texts look like?
options: A tree of tags in angle brackets
A Python dictionary and list with a few changes
why: JSON text looks like a Python dictionary and list with a few changes.

q: How does JSON write the Python values None, True and False?
options: None, True and False as in Python
null, true and false in lowercase
why: JSON writes missing as null and the booleans as true and false, in lowercase.

q: What does the chapter's reading of JSON turn JSON text into?
options: Python values such as dictionaries and lists
why: Reading JSON gives back the Python value, a dictionary for an object.

q: Which function takes a string of JSON text and returns the Python value?
why: json.loads takes a string; json.load does the same for a file.

q: What does json.loads raise for text that is not valid JSON?
why: JSONDecodeError is a kind of ValueError and carries the message and the position of the fault.

q: Which function writes a Python value as JSON text?
options: json.print, which prints to the screen
why: Writing JSON turns a Python value into text with json.dumps.

q: What does indent=2 do to the output of json.dumps?
options: It keeps only the first two items
It adds two spaces after every comma on one line
It writes two copies of the text
It puts each item and member on its own line, indented by two spaces per level
why: The indent option puts each array item and member on its own line, indented that many spaces per level.

q: What does running the json module as a script do?
options: It checks JSON text and prints it indented, or reports where it is invalid
It converts JSON text into XML
It starts a web server for JSON files
It compiles JSON text into Python code
why: The chapter's python -m json checks JSON text from a file or standard input and prints it indented.

q: What happens to a Python tuple that goes through json.dumps and then json.loads?
options: It comes back as a tuple
It comes back as a string
It comes back as a list
why: JSON has arrays but no tuples, so a tuple comes back as a list.

q: What happens when json.dumps is given a set?
options: It writes the set as a JSON array
It raises TypeError, so the program converts the set first
It writes the set as a string
why: A value outside the basic types raises TypeError and is converted by the program first.

q: What does XML mark its data with?
options: Elements written between tags, which may have attributes
why: XML is the chapter's third format and is read with ElementTree.

q: Which rule does an XML document follow?
options: It has exactly one root element that holds all the others
Every element must have an attribute
Every value is written in quotes
why: A valid XML document has one root element.

q: Two elements side by side at the top of a text make it...
options: A valid XML document with two roots
why: A valid XML document has one root element, so two elements side by side at the top is not valid.

q: Which module does the chapter use to read XML?
why: ElementTree reads XML text or a file into Element objects.

q: What does ET.fromstring return?
why: ET.fromstring returns the root Element; ET.parse returns an ElementTree.

q: How does a program visit the children of an Element?
options: It indexes the Element like a list or loops over it
why: An Element is indexed like a list of its children and looped over for the children.

q: How is an XML document built from scratch with ElementTree?
options: A dictionary is passed to json.dumps
A root is made with Element and children are added with SubElement
A list of rows is given to a writer
why: A document is built by making a root with Element and adding children with SubElement.

q: Which call sets the attribute first of an element to Alice?
why: The set method sets an attribute; the text attribute sets the text.

q: What is the difference between the DOM and SAX approaches?
options: DOM is for CSV, SAX is for JSON
DOM writes files, SAX reads them
DOM loads the whole document into memory, SAX reads a stream of events
why: The DOM approach loads the whole document into memory and the SAX approach reads it as a stream of events.

q: Which ElementTree function lets a program read a document in steps?
why: ElementTree offers the tree plus iterparse for reading in steps.

q: Why does the chapter's topic of entity expansion matter for data from untrusted sources?
options: A short document can expand into a very large text
why: An XML document can define entities that the parser expands, so a short document can become a very large text.

q: What type is the value of an element's text in ElementTree?
options: An int when it looks like a number
A string, which the program converts with int or float
A bool when it says true
A float when it has a dot
why: XML holds only text, so a program converts values itself.

q: What does the third-party xmltodict do with attributes?
options: It gives them keys with an @ prefix in nested dictionaries
why: xmltodict turns XML text into nested dictionaries with @-prefixed keys for attributes; it was not executed here.

q: Which two things best decide the format for a piece of data?
options: The shape and the types of the data
The length of the file name only
why: The chapter is best taught as a choice of format by the shape and the types of the data.

q: Which format gives back the number 30 as an int when it reads it?
why: CSV and XML give back the text 30, and json.loads gives the int 30.

q: What do the chapter's practice questions ask about?
options: What Excel has that CSV lacks, what the reader and writer take, and how JSON writes null and booleans
How to connect to a database
why: The practice questions cover Excel against CSV, the reader and writer, and JSON null and booleans.

q: What does csv.reader take?
options: A File object, or an iterable of lines, not a file name
why: A reader is given a File object, not a file name.

q: How are the output files of the practice program named?
options: From the workbook name without its extension and the sheet title
From the date of the run
From the first cell of each sheet
why: The practice program writes one CSV file per sheet, named from the workbook name and the sheet title.

q: In Python 3.14, what do the notes on a TypeError from json.dumps name?
options: The line number of the program
The name of the file being written
The dictionary keys and list positions leading to the value that could not be written
why: Since Python 3.14 the TypeError carries notes naming the keys and positions that lead to the unwritable value.

q: Which module reads TOML in the standard library, and can it write TOML?
options: tomllib reads TOML and has no dumps function
why: tomllib has loads and load but no dumps.
